sentences.sentence: Reward models that score robot rollouts are also used as failure detectors, and we compared two zero-shot reward models with plain episode length.
On ArmnetBench, a public SO-101 benchmark where runs end at a time limit, length separates failure from success at AUROC 0.942 within policy.
Failed runs there are slow rather than cut off, and length observed only up to half of the longest episode still gives 0.851.
Both reward models score below length, the better one at 0.821.
On our own rollouts, which an operator stopped by judgment, length falls to 0.56 and neither reward model beats the identity of the policy.
A judge that sees the finished episode passes its threshold there, at an operating point chosen in-sample, and no mid-episode monitor reaches its bar.
The baseline a detector has to beat depends on the dataset's stopping rule.
Papers that evaluate a reward model as a failure detector usually compare it with other learned detectors.
When a benchmark stops failed runs at a time limit, the length of an episode also encodes its outcome, and so can the identity of the policy that ran (we call this the policy-identity null).
When an operator stops each run by judgment, both signals are weaker.
We call the way a dataset ends its episodes its *stopping rule*.
None of the reward-model papers in our library reports the stopping rule or a length baseline.

We started with a narrower claim, that elapsed time is the reward model to beat, and our own rollouts did not support it: on them length is near chance, and a robot-trained judge passed its pre-registered threshold.
The stopping rule separates the two results, so it became the subject of the paper.
We measured length on ArmnetBench and on our own rollouts, with the length analyses frozen before any number existed.
We compared it with two zero-shot reward models, Robometer and TOPReward, and on our 88 operator-stopped rollouts also with every judge and monitor we had run.
ArmnetBench v0.1 has 8 tasks and 7 policies on the SO-101.
We use its 2,047 policy rollouts with a success or failure class (515 successes, 1,532 failures) and leave out the teleoperated episodes.
One task, pushing a Displayport cable (270 rollouts), has rollouts of a single class and so no per-task AUROC.
Our own data are 88 labelled bowls-task episodes on one SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX, and every monitor gate used the same 50-episode subset (42 successes, 8 failures).
The author was the operator, who stopped each run and labelled it at rest, not blind to the policy.
On ArmnetBench, episode length is a strong failure detector within each policy (Table 1, Fig. 1).
Pooled over policies it reaches 0.938, and within each policy it ranges from 0.91 to 0.96.
Pair-weighted, the within-policy value is 0.942, with a CI of 0.927–0.956.
We ran Robometer-4B zero-shot, as its authors ship it, and it scores 0.818 pooled and 0.821 within policy.
The within-policy value is pair-weighted over its per-policy scores, whose range stands in for a CI (§7).
TOPReward, run with Qwen3-VL-8B and no training, scores 0.661 within policy, and its paired difference to length has a 95 % CI of -0.31 to -0.25.
The protocols fixed each model's primary score before any score existed: the success probability for Robometer and the success score of its paper for TOPReward.
Two other scores from the same runs, listed in Table 1 as descriptive rows, are higher and still below length.

Robometer scales a general-purpose reward model through trajectory comparisons, and TOPReward reads the token probabilities of a video-language model as hidden rewards.
A survey of verifiers for robot policies covers the wider family.
FAIL-Detect and SAFE learn uncertainty- and feature-based failure scores for imitation and VLA policies.
FARM reads failure signals from the internal states of a frozen world model, as our world-model monitors do, and our risk head follows ReAP, which predicts action-conditioned risk.
VLA-Corrector verifies stages, Spotter adds a reflecting VLM, and REMORA tracks progress through errors and recovery.
ArmnetBench and a standardized SO-101 VLA benchmark evaluate policies on the same arm.
None of these works reports the elapsed-length baseline under the dataset's stopping rule.
The judge pass on our own rollouts rests on 8 failures and on operating thresholds chosen on the same 50 episodes, which a single operator, the author, labelled without being blind to the policy.
The threshold-free AUROCs do not depend on the threshold, and fresh rollouts scored at the frozen thresholds would confirm the operating points.
17 of the 25 failures in our 69 rollouts are TurboVLA's, so any score that reads the policy gets the policy-identity null for free.
The risk head is trained and tested on the same 50 episodes, with five folds by episode that keep episodes from leaking (tasks and policies do leak).
Robometer's per-episode scores stayed on an older machine.
Its within-policy number therefore has no episode-bootstrap CI and it is missing from the truncation analysis, and a copy from that machine or a re-score of about $6 would restore both.
TOPReward's paper does not give its prefix count, frames per query or Yes/No wording, so those are our choices.
The ArmnetBench result covers eight tasks, and the timeout is approximated by each task's longest episode.
On ArmnetBench, where runs end at a time limit, episode length beat both reward models.
On our operator-stopped rollouts length was at chance, and a judge that saw the whole finished episode caught the failures.
When you evaluate a reward model as a failure detector, report episode length within policy on the same rows and say how the episodes ended.
